landshut.name: Landshut
landshut.summary: A town in Bavaria, Germany, on the River Isar; it is the capital of Lower Bavaria and, with over 75,000 people, its largest city.

transylvanian-saxons.name: Transylvanian Saxons
transylvanian-saxons.summary: A Germanic people who settled Transylvania from the 12th century onward, mostly from Flanders, Luxembourg and nearby regions, among the oldest German-speaking communities in Central-Eastern Europe.

hyacinth-of-poland.name: Saint Hyacinth of Poland
hyacinth-of-poland.summary: A Polish Dominican priest and missionary, about 1185 to 1257, venerated as a saint for reforming women's monasteries in Poland.

kievan-rus.name: Kievan Rus'
kievan-rus.summary: The first East Slavic state, later a group of principalities, spanning the late 9th to mid-13th century from the White Sea to the Black Sea under the Rurik dynasty.

martin-schongauer.name: Martin Schongauer
martin-schongauer.summary: Alsatian engraver and painter (c. 1450–1491), the most important printmaker north of the Alps before Albrecht Dürer, whose 116 surviving engravings were known across Europe.

imperial-crown-of-the-holy-roman-empire.name: Imperial Crown of the Holy Roman Empire
imperial-crown-of-the-holy-roman-empire.summary: Octagonal coronation crown of the Holy Roman Emperor, probably made in the late 10th century and used until the empire's dissolution in 1806; now kept in Vienna.
imperial-crown-of-the-holy-roman-empire.source_title: Imperial Crown of the Holy Roman Empire

hofburg.name: Hofburg
hofburg.summary: The former principal imperial palace of the Habsburg dynasty in Vienna, built in the 13th century and today the official residence of Austria's president.

st-michael-s-church-hildesheim.name: St. Michael's Church, Hildesheim
st-michael-s-church-hildesheim.summary: An early-Romanesque church in Hildesheim, Germany, a UNESCO World Heritage site since 1985 for its architecture and artworks such as the Tree of Jesse.

bernward-of-hildesheim.name: Bishop Bernward
bernward-of-hildesheim.summary: Thirteenth Bishop of Hildesheim, holding the office from 993 until his death in 1022.

ottonian-architecture.name: Ottonian Architecture
ottonian-architecture.summary: An architectural style, mostly seen in churches, that developed under Emperor Otto the Great in Germany and the Low Countries from the mid 10th to mid 11th century.

kammerzell-house.name: Kammerzell House
kammerzell-house.summary: One of the most famous buildings in Strasbourg, France, and one of the best-preserved medieval civil buildings in late-Gothic style, built in 1427.

adelaide-of-italy.name: Adelaide of Italy
adelaide-of-italy.summary: Holy Roman Empress (931–999) by marriage to Otto the Great, crowned in Rome in 962; later regent of the empire for her grandson from 991 to 995, and a model for future royal consorts.

meissen-cathedral.name: Meissen Cathedral
meissen-cathedral.summary: A Gothic church on the castle hill of Meissen, Saxony, standing beside Albrechtsburg castle overlooking the River Elbe.

conrad-iii-of-germany.name: Conrad III
conrad-iii-of-germany.summary: King of the Romans in the Holy Roman Empire from 1138 to 1152, of the Hohenstaufen dynasty, who led German forces in the failed Second Crusade.

romanesque-architecture.name: Romanesque architecture
romanesque-architecture.summary: A medieval European architectural style of the 11th and 12th centuries marked by rounded arches, thick walls and sturdy pillars, which later developed into the Gothic style.

wawel-cathedral.name: Crypt of Saint Leonard
wawel-cathedral.summary: Part of the nearly 1,000-year-old Wawel Cathedral in Kraków, the coronation site of Polish monarchs, which combines Romanesque, Gothic, Renaissance and Baroque architecture.

wawel-castle.name: Wawel Hill
wawel-castle.summary: The fortified hill above the Vistula River in Kraków holding Wawel Castle, the residence and symbol of Polish statehood since the Middle Ages, with structures dating back to 970 CE.

p-ock-cathedral.name: Płock Cathedral
p-ock-cathedral.summary: A 12th-century Romanesque cathedral in Płock, Poland, built in 1144 and the oldest historical monument in the city.

gniezno-doors.name: Gniezno Doors
gniezno-doors.summary: Bronze doors at Gniezno Cathedral in Poland, made around 1175, showing eighteen scenes from the life of Saint Adalbert and ranking among Poland's finest Romanesque artworks.

adalbert-of-prague.name: Saint Adalbert
adalbert-of-prague.summary: Czech missionary and bishop of Prague (c.956–997), martyred while converting the Baltic Prussians; later declared patron saint of the Czech Republic and Poland.

charles-iv-holy-roman-emperor.name: Charles IV, Holy Roman Emperor
charles-iv-holy-roman-emperor.summary: Holy Roman Emperor from 1355 until his death in 1378, also King of Bohemia and King of the Romans; born in 1316 as Wenceslaus, son of John of Bohemia.

karl-tejn.name: Karlštejn Castle
karl-tejn.summary: A large Gothic castle in Czechia founded in 1348 by King Charles IV to safeguard the Imperial Regalia and Bohemian crown jewels.

mainz-cathedral.name: Mainz Cathedral
mainz-cathedral.summary: 1,000-year-old Roman Catholic cathedral in Mainz, Germany, and seat of the Bishop of Mainz, built mainly in the Romanesque style.

sandomierz.name: Sandomierz
sandomierz.summary: A historic town in south-eastern Poland on the Vistula River, once a royal city of the Polish Crown and a major regional centre from the Middle Ages to the 19th century.

iwo-odrow.name: Iwo Odrowąż
iwo-odrow.summary: A medieval Polish humanist, statesman and bishop who died in 1229.

brick-gothic.name: Brick Gothic
brick-gothic.summary: A style of Gothic architecture built in brick, common around the Baltic Sea in Northeast and Central Europe from the 12th century, marked by an absence of figurative stone sculpture.

sigismund-holy-roman-emperor.name: Sigismund, Holy Roman Emperor
sigismund-holy-roman-emperor.summary: King of Hungary from 1387, King of Germany from 1410, and Holy Roman Emperor from 1433 until his death in 1437, who led the failed Crusade of Nicopolis and was a driving force behind the Council of Constance.

hussite-wars.name: Hussite Wars
hussite-wars.summary: A series of civil wars, 1419 to about 1434, between followers of the executed reformer Jan Hus and Catholic forces led by Holy Roman Emperor Sigismund.

visegr-d-hungary.name: Visegrád
visegr-d-hungary.summary: Castle town north of Budapest, Hungary, on the Danube, site of a medieval citadel and King Matthias Corvinus's Renaissance summer palace; it also gave its name to the 1991 Visegrád Group.

heilig-geist-spital.name: Heilig-Geist-Spital
heilig-geist-spital.summary: The largest hospital in the former Free Imperial City of Nuremberg, whose chapel housed the Holy Roman Empire's crown jewels from 1424 to 1796.

landfrieden.name: Landfrieden
landfrieden.summary: Under Holy Roman Empire law, a contractual waiver by territorial rulers of the use of force to assert their own legal claims, especially affecting the right of feuding.

henry-vii-holy-roman-emperor.name: Henry VII, Holy Roman Emperor
henry-vii-holy-roman-emperor.summary: King of Germany from 1308 and Holy Roman Emperor from 1312, the first of the House of Luxembourg, who ended the Great Interregnum but died suddenly while campaigning in Italy.

iron-crown.name: Iron Crown
iron-crown.summary: A medieval reliquary crown of gold and jewels around a central band traditionally said to be forged from a nail of the True Cross, used to crown some Holy Roman Emperors as kings of Italy.

guelphs-and-ghibellines.name: Guelphs
guelphs-and-ghibellines.summary: A faction supporting the Pope against the Holy Roman Emperor's Ghibelline supporters, dominating politics in medieval Italian city-states during the 12th and 13th centuries.

matteo-i-visconti.name: Matteo I Visconti
matteo-i-visconti.summary: Ruler of Milan from 1295 to 1322 who expanded Visconti influence across northern Italy before being excommunicated on a charge of necromancy and resigning.

old-swiss-confederacy.name: Old Swiss Confederacy
old-swiss-confederacy.summary: A confederation of small independent states, precursor to modern Switzerland, that formed in the late 13th century and grew from eight to thirteen cantons by 1513.

saint-george-s-cross.name: St George's Cross
saint-george-s-cross.summary: A red cross on a white background, associated with Saint George since the Late Middle Ages; it later became the national flag of England.

pope-innocent-iv.name: Pope Innocent IV
pope-innocent-iv.summary: Head of the Catholic Church and Papal States from 1243 to 1254, a noted canonist whose dispute with Emperor Frederick II forced him to flee to France; he later authorized torture against heretics.

frederick-ii-holy-roman-emperor.name: Frederick II, Holy Roman Emperor
frederick-ii-holy-roman-emperor.summary: King of Sicily, Germany, Italy and Jerusalem, and Holy Roman Emperor from 1220 to 1250, ruling from Sicily to Germany and repeatedly clashing with the papacy, which excommunicated him four times.

henry-raspe.name: Henry Raspe
henry-raspe.summary: Landgrave of Thuringia elected King of Germany in 1246 against Conrad IV with papal backing, though his contested reign lasted only nine months before his death in 1247.

conrad-iv-of-germany.name: Conrad IV
conrad-iv-of-germany.summary: King of Germany, Italy, Jerusalem, and Sicily (1228–1254), son of Emperor Frederick II, who ruled amid ongoing conflict following his father's deposition.

conrad-ii-holy-roman-emperor.name: Conrad II
conrad-ii-holy-roman-emperor.summary: First of the Salian emperors of the Holy Roman Empire (c. 990–1039), who ruled Germany, Italy, and Burgundy and founded a dynasty that lasted a century.

henry-iii-holy-roman-emperor.name: Henry III, Holy Roman Emperor
henry-iii-holy-roman-emperor.summary: Holy Roman Emperor from 1046 to 1056, a Salian ruler who ended a papal schism, was crowned by Pope Clement II, and tightened royal control over the German duchies.

william-ii-of-holland.name: William of Holland
william-ii-of-holland.summary: Count of Holland and Zeeland from 1234, elected anti-king of Germany in 1248 and ruled as sole king from 1254 until his death in 1256.

ulrich-iii-of-w-rttemberg.name: Ulrich III of Württemberg
ulrich-iii-of-w-rttemberg.summary: Count of Württemberg from 1325 until his death in 1344.

house-of-w-rttemberg.name: House of Württemberg
house-of-w-rttemberg.summary: An ancient German dynasty and former royal family that ruled the Kingdom of Württemberg.

old-high-german-literature.name: Old High German literature
old-high-german-literature.summary: Literature written in Old High German from the 8th to mid-11th century, produced almost entirely in monasteries and religious in nature.

middle-high-german.name: Middle High German
middle-high-german.summary: The stage of the German language conventionally dated from 1050 to 1350, developing from Old High German into Early New High German.

early-new-high-german.name: Early New High German
early-new-high-german.summary: A period in the history of the German language, generally dated 1350 to 1650, between Middle High German and modern New High German.

nibelungenlied.name: Nibelungenlied
nibelungenlied.summary: An epic poem written around 1200 in Middle High German, based on oral Germanic heroic legend, telling of Siegfried, Kriemhild and the destruction of Etzel's Hunnic kingdom.

oswald-von-wolkenstein.name: Oswald von Wolkenstein
oswald-von-wolkenstein.summary: Poet, composer and diplomat (1376/77–1445) who traveled across Europe as far as Georgia and was inducted into several knightly orders.

johannes-von-tepl.name: Johannes von Tepl
johannes-von-tepl.summary: Bohemian writer (c. 1350–c. 1415), among the earliest prose writers in Early New High German, best known for the poem Der Ackermann aus Böhmen, a dialogue between Death and a ploughman.

pontus-and-sidonia.name: Pontus and Sidonia
pontus-and-sidonia.summary: A medieval prose romance composed in French around 1400, about Pontus, son of the king of Galicia, who falls in love with Sidonia, daughter of the king of Brittany.

notker-labeo.name: Notker Labeo
notker-labeo.summary: A Benedictine monk and scholar, c. 950 to 1022, the first medieval commentator on Aristotle, who translated earlier Latin works into Old High German.

sebastian-brant.name: Sebastian Brant
sebastian-brant.summary: A German humanist and satirist (1457/58-1521), best known for his satire The Ship of Fools.

ship-of-fools-satire.name: Ship of Fools
ship-of-fools-satire.summary: A 1494 satirical allegory in German verse by Sebastian Brant, the most famous work built on the 'ship of fools' trope, widely translated across Europe.

hans-folz.name: Hans Folz
hans-folz.summary: German author and Nuremberg master barber (c. 1437–1513) who reformed meistersang poetry, writing about a thousand songs and satirical plays, some with harshly antisemitic content.

chapbook.name: Volksbuch (chapbook)
chapbook.summary: German name for the chapbook tradition, cheaply printed booklets of popular street literature that flourished in early modern Europe from the 16th century.

johannes-gutenberg.name: Johannes Gutenberg
johannes-gutenberg.summary: German inventor (c. 1393–1468) of the movable-type printing press, whose innovations in type-casting and oil-based ink enabled the Gutenberg Bible and are credited with sparking an information revolution across Europe.

albertus-magnus.name: Albertus Magnus
albertus-magnus.summary: German Dominican friar, philosopher, scientist and bishop (c. 1200–1280), considered one of the greatest medieval thinkers and canonized in 1931.

rudolf-iv-of-austria.name: Rudolf IV of Austria
rudolf-iv-of-austria.summary: Habsburg duke of Austria (1339–1365), also called Rudolf the Founder. He commissioned the forged Privilegium Maius to raise Austria's rulers to higher titles and began using the archducal title in 1359.

university-of-vienna.name: University of Vienna
university-of-vienna.summary: Public research university in Vienna, Austria, founded in 1365. It has around 85,000 students and has been home to scholars such as Schrödinger, Freud, Mendel and Popper.

georg-von-peuerbach.name: Georg von Peuerbach
georg-von-peuerbach.summary: Austrian astronomer, poet, mathematician and instrument maker (1423-1461). He helped make astronomy, mathematics and literature simple and accessible to Europeans during the Renaissance.

doctor-of-the-church.name: Doctor of the Church
doctor-of-the-church.summary: A title given by the Catholic Church to saints recognized for major contributions to theology or doctrine; 38 had been named as of 2025.

bessarion.name: Bessarion
bessarion.summary: Byzantine Greek humanist, theologian and Catholic cardinal (1403 to 1472) who helped revive letters in the 15th century. Educated by Gemistus Pletho, he was twice considered for the papacy.

regiomontanus.name: Regiomontanus
regiomontanus.summary: German Renaissance mathematician, astrologer and astronomer (1436–1476), born Johannes Müller von Königsberg. Active in Vienna, Buda and Nuremberg, his work helped pave the way for Copernican heliocentrism.

ptolemy.name: Ptolemy
ptolemy.summary: A Greco-Roman scholar of the 2nd century AD who wrote influential works on astronomy, geography and astrology; his geocentric model of the universe, promoted by the Catholic Church, was studied for over a thousand years.

almagest.name: Almagest
almagest.summary: Ptolemy's 2nd-century astronomical treatise that established the geocentric model of the universe, accepted for over 1,200 years.

bernhard-walther.name: Bernhard Walther
bernhard-walther.summary: Wealthy German merchant, humanist and astronomer (1430 to 1504) based in Nuremberg. After Regiomontanus died in 1476 he bought his instruments and kept observing the planets until his death.

type-metal.name: Type metal
type-metal.summary: Alloy of lead, tin and antimony used in traditional typefounding and hot metal typesetting. Antimony and tin add durability, and the alloy must cast sharply and keep its shape as it cools.

nicholas-of-cusa.name: Nicholas of Cusa
nicholas-of-cusa.summary: German bishop and polymath (1401–1464), an early German proponent of Renaissance humanism known for his mystical writings on "learned ignorance".

bernkastel-kues.name: Kues
bernkastel-kues.summary: Winegrowing town on the Middle Mosel in Rhineland-Palatinate, Germany, now part of Bernkastel-Kues. It is the birthplace of the medieval churchman and philosopher Nikolaus von Kues, known as Cusanus.

de-docta-ignorantia.name: On Learned Ignorance
de-docta-ignorantia.summary: Latin title De docta ignorantia. Earlier thinkers such as Augustine had spoken of a "learned ignorance", and this book argues that both reason and understanding beyond reason are needed to grasp God.

george-of-trebizond.name: George of Trebizond
george-of-trebizond.summary: Byzantine Greek philosopher, scholar and humanist (1395-1486).

nicolaus-copernicus.name: Nicolaus Copernicus
nicolaus-copernicus.summary: Renaissance polymath (1473–1543) who proposed that the Sun, not Earth, is at the center of the universe, triggering the Copernican Revolution.

heidelberg-university.name: Heidelberg University
heidelberg-university.summary: Public research university in Baden-Württemberg, Germany, and the country's oldest. It was the third university founded in the Holy Roman Empire, and 33 Nobel Prize winners have been affiliated with it.

marsilius-of-inghen.name: Marsilius of Inghen
marsilius-of-inghen.summary: Dutch philosopher (c. 1340–1396) who studied with Albert of Saxony and Nicole Oresme under Jean Buridan, and was Magister at the University of Paris as well as at the University of Heidelberg from 1386 to 1396.

hartmann-schedel.name: Hartmann Schedel
hartmann-schedel.summary: German historian, physician and humanist (1440-1514) from Nuremberg, and one of the first cartographers to use the printing press. He is best known for writing the text of the Nuremberg Chronicle, published in 1493.

astrolabe.name: Astrolabe
astrolabe.summary: An ancient astronomical instrument and star chart used to measure the altitude of celestial bodies and to determine time, latitude, or position.

prince-elector.name: Prince-elector
prince-elector.summary: A member of the Electoral College of the Holy Roman Empire who elected the Holy Roman Emperor, a privileged office that existed until the empire's dissolution in 1806.

golden-bull-of-1356.name: Golden Bull of 1356
golden-bull-of-1356.summary: Imperial decree issued under Emperor Charles IV that fixed key constitutional rules of the Holy Roman Empire, including its seven prince-electors, for over four centuries.

interregnum-holy-roman-empire.name: The Interregnum (Holy Roman Empire)
interregnum-holy-roman-empire.summary: A period with no reigning emperor in the Holy Roman Empire, including a 62-year gap between 1250 and 1312 following Frederick II's death, ending with Rudolf I's election.

rudolf-i-of-germany.name: Rudolf I
rudolf-i-of-germany.summary: A German nobleman and the first Habsburg to become King of the Romans, reigning from 1273 until his death in 1291; he defeated Ottokar II of Bohemia and secured Habsburg control of Austria, Styria and Carinthia.

house-of-habsburg.name: Habsburg dynasty
house-of-habsburg.summary: One of Europe's most powerful dynasties, ruling the Holy Roman Empire, Austria and Spain from the Middle Ages until its male line ended in 1740.

kaiserpfalz.name: Kaiserpfalz
kaiserpfalz.summary: Imperial palace or castle across the Holy Roman Empire used as a temporary seat of power by the emperor during his travels in the Early and High Middle Ages.

declaration-of-rhense.name: Declaration of Rhense
declaration-of-rhense.summary: A 1338 agreement among the prince-electors of the Holy Roman Empire declaring that their election alone, without papal approval, made a king legitimate.

otto-iii-holy-roman-emperor.name: Otto III
otto-iii-holy-roman-emperor.summary: Holy Roman Emperor and King of Italy from 996 until his death in 1002, crowned King of Germany at age three and long governed through regents before ruling himself.

congress-of-gniezno.name: Congress of Gniezno
congress-of-gniezno.summary: A meeting in the year 1000 between Polish Duke Bolesław I the Brave and Emperor Otto III at Gniezno, of disputed significance for Poland's royal status.

archdiocese-of-gniezno.name: Archdiocese of Gniezno
archdiocese-of-gniezno.summary: The oldest Latin Catholic archdiocese in Poland, based in the city of Gniezno.

piast-dynasty.name: Piast dynasty
piast-dynasty.summary: The first historical ruling dynasty of Poland, beginning with Duke Mieszko I around 960 and ending royal rule in 1370 with the death of King Casimir III the Great.

boles-aw-i-the-brave.name: Bolesław I the Brave
boles-aw-i-the-brave.summary: Duke of Poland from 992 and its first King in 1025, of the Piast dynasty, who reunified Poland and promoted Western Christianity.

rudolph-iii-of-burgundy.name: Rudolph III of Burgundy
rudolph-iii-of-burgundy.summary: King of Burgundy from 993 until his death in 1032, the last ruler of an independent Kingdom of Burgundy and the last legitimate male of its Elder House of Welf line.

henry-ii-holy-roman-emperor.name: Henry II, Holy Roman Emperor
henry-ii-holy-roman-emperor.summary: Holy Roman Emperor from 1014 to 1024, the last ruler of the Ottonian dynasty, who died without an heir and was later canonized as a saint.

kingdom-of-arles.name: Kingdom of Burgundy
kingdom-of-arles.summary: Also called the Kingdom of Arles, a realm formed in 933 by uniting Lower and Upper Burgundy, later becoming one of the three constituent kingdoms of the Holy Roman Empire.

scholasticism.name: Scholasticism
scholasticism.summary: Medieval European method of philosophical and theological study, dominant from about 1100 to 1700, using rigorous logical debate to reconcile Aristotle's philosophy with Christian theology.

nicomachean-ethics.name: Nicomachean Ethics
nicomachean-ethics.summary: Aristotle's best-known work on ethics, exploring how to live well and what constitutes the good; hugely influential on medieval philosophy.

hildegard-of-bingen.name: Hildegard von Bingen
hildegard-of-bingen.summary: A German Benedictine abbess (c. 1098-1179) called the 'Sibyl of the Rhine,' a writer, composer, mystic and polymath regarded as a founder of scientific natural history in Germany.

neoplatonism.name: Neoplatonism
neoplatonism.summary: A version of Platonic philosophy emerging in the 3rd century AD, holding that reality derives from a single principle, 'the One,' and influencing later Christian, Jewish and Muslim thought.

scivias.name: Scivias
scivias.summary: Illustrated work by Hildegard von Bingen, completed 1151-52, recording 26 religious visions, divided into three parts on creation, salvation and the coming kingdom of God.

albert-of-saxony-philosopher.name: Albert of Saxony
albert-of-saxony-philosopher.summary: German philosopher and mathematician (c. 1320–1390) known for contributions to logic and physics, and bishop of Halberstadt from 1366 until his death.

meister-eckhart.name: Meister Eckhart
meister-eckhart.summary: German Catholic priest, theologian, and mystic (c. 1260–c. 1328) of the Dominican Order, tried for heresy by Pope John XXII shortly before his death.

henry-suso.name: Henry Suso
henry-suso.summary: German Dominican friar (1295–1366) and popular vernacular writer known for defending the theologian Meister Eckhart after his posthumous condemnation for heresy.

friends-of-god.name: Friends of God
friends-of-god.summary: A medieval mystical group of clergy and laypeople within the Catholic Church, founded around 1339–1343 and centered in Basel, Switzerland.

john-of-ruusbroec.name: John of Ruusbroec
john-of-ruusbroec.summary: Augustinian canon (1293/94–1381), one of the most important medieval mystics of the Low Countries, who wrote his works in Middle Dutch rather than Latin to reach a wider audience.

saint-emmeram-s-abbey.name: St. Emmeram's Abbey
saint-emmeram-s-abbey.summary: Benedictine monastery founded around 739 in Regensburg, Bavaria, at the grave of the Frankish bishop Saint Emmeram.

otloh-of-sankt-emmeram.name: Otloh of Sankt Emmeram
otloh-of-sankt-emmeram.summary: Benedictine monk, composer, writer and music theorist at St Emmeram's monastery in Regensburg, active from about 1010 to 1072.

manegold-of-lautenbach.name: Manegold of Lautenbach
manegold-of-lautenbach.summary: An Augustinian canon and polemical writer from Alsace (c. 1030–c. 1103), active as a teacher in south-west Germany and one of the first recognised masters of theology.

theodoric-of-freiberg.name: Theodoric of Freiberg
theodoric-of-freiberg.summary: German Dominican theologian, philosopher and physicist (c. 1250–1311) who became provincial of the Dominican Order in 1293.

thomas-aquinas.name: Thomas Aquinas
thomas-aquinas.summary: An Italian Dominican friar, theologian and philosopher (c. 1225–1274) who blended Aristotelian philosophy with Christian doctrine and founded the school of thought called Thomism.

william-of-moerbeke.name: William of Moerbeke
william-of-moerbeke.summary: William of Moerbeke: 13th-century translator who rendered Greek philosophical, medical and scientific texts into Latin; his translations were influential and are still respected by modern scholars.

northern-renaissance.name: Northern Renaissance
northern-renaissance.summary: Cultural awakening in Europe north of the Alps that developed later than the Italian Renaissance, mostly beginning in the late 15th century, taking distinct forms in Germany, France, England, the Low Countries and Poland.

johann-heynlin.name: Johann Heynlin
johann-heynlin.summary: German-born scholar, humanist and theologian (c. 1425–1496) who introduced the first printing press to France, setting one up in Paris in 1470.

brethren-of-the-common-life.name: Brethren of the Common Life
brethren-of-the-common-life.summary: Roman Catholic pietist community founded in the 14th-century Netherlands by Gerard Groote, promoting simple, practical devotion to Christ in everyday life without formal monastic vows.

thomas-kempis.name: Thomas à Kempis
thomas-kempis.summary: A German-Dutch Augustinian canon (c. 1380–1471) and author of The Imitation of Christ, a leading Christian devotional book, linked to the Modern Devotion reform movement.

devotio-moderna.name: Devotio Moderna
devotio-moderna.summary: A late 14th-century religious reform movement in the Low Countries and Germany emphasizing humility and simplicity, best known for influencing Thomas à Kempis, author of The Imitation of Christ.

the-imitation-of-christ.name: The Imitation of Christ
the-imitation-of-christ.summary: A Christian devotional book written around 1418–1427, emphasizing the interior life and devotion to the Eucharist; among the most widely read Christian works after the Bible.

berthold-of-moosburg.name: Berthold of Moosburg
berthold-of-moosburg.summary: German Dominican monk and 14th-century theologian and neo-Platonist, active from 1316 to 1361, who succeeded Meister Eckhart as head of the Cologne Dominicans in 1335.

johannes-tauler.name: Johannes Tauler
johannes-tauler.summary: German mystic, Catholic priest and Dominican theologian (c. 1300–1361), considered one of the most important Rhineland mystics.

heymeric-de-campo.name: Heymeric de Campo
heymeric-de-campo.summary: Dutch theologian and scholastic philosopher (1395–1460), a leading Albertist and forerunner of Nicholas of Cusa who taught at Cologne and Leuven and wrote on universals and the Apocalypse.

henry-of-langenstein.name: Henry of Langenstein
henry-of-langenstein.summary: German scholastic philosopher, theologian and mathematician who lived from around 1325 to 1397.

henry-of-oyta.name: Henry of Oyta
henry-of-oyta.summary: German theologian and nominalist philosopher who lived from around 1330 to 1397.

william-of-ockham.name: William of Ockham
william-of-ockham.summary: English Franciscan friar and scholastic philosopher (c. 1287–1347), one of the major figures of medieval thought and namesake of Occam's razor.

conciliarism.name: Conciliarism
conciliarism.summary: A 14th- to 16th-century Catholic Church movement holding that supreme church authority rests with an ecumenical council rather than the pope, emerging from the Western Schism.

studium-generale.name: Studium generale
studium-generale.summary: The traditional medieval term for a university in medieval Europe.

lambertus-de-monte.name: Lambertus de Monte
lambertus-de-monte.summary: A medieval scholastic and Thomist (c. 1430/5-1499) who taught at the University of Cologne and defended Thomas Aquinas's reading of Aristotle, even arguing for Aristotle's salvation.

thomism.name: Thomism
thomism.summary: The philosophical and theological school built on the work of Thomas Aquinas, whose writings remain central to Catholic philosophy and theology.

ostsiedlung.name: Ostsiedlung
ostsiedlung.summary: The medieval eastward migration and Germanization of Slavic, Baltic and Uralic lands by ethnic Germans, reshaping settlement across Central and Eastern Europe.

martin-of-opava.name: Martin of Opava
martin-of-opava.summary: 13th-century Dominican friar, bishop and chronicler who died in 1278, also known as Martin of Poland (Martinus Polonus).

vitello.name: Witelo
vitello.summary: Polish friar, scientist, theologian and natural philosopher (c. 1230 – 1280/1314), an important figure in the history of philosophy in Poland.

jagiellonian-university.name: Jagiellonian University
jagiellonian-university.summary: Public university in Kraków founded in 1364 by King Casimir III the Great, the oldest university in Poland and among the oldest continuously operating in the world.

stanis-aw-of-skarbimierz.name: Stanisław of Skarbimierz
stanis-aw-of-skarbimierz.summary: First rector of the restored University of Krakow from 1399, whose sermons on just war helped frame Poland's position at the Council of Constance.

pawe-w-odkowic.name: Paweł Włodkowic
pawe-w-odkowic.summary: A Polish scholar, jurist and rector of the Kraków Academy, about 1370 to 1435, who argued for religious tolerance and defended Poland against the Teutonic Knights.

jan-of-g-og-w.name: Jan of Głogów
jan-of-g-og-w.summary: Polish scholar (c. 1445–1507) active at the turn of the Middle Ages and Renaissance, working as a philosopher, geographer and astronomer at the University of Krakow.

albert-brudzewski.name: Albert Brudzewski
albert-brudzewski.summary: Polish astronomer, philosopher and diplomat (c.1445–c.1497) who modernized astronomy teaching and was an influential teacher of Nicolaus Copernicus.

kingdom-of-germany.name: Kingdom of Germany
kingdom-of-germany.summary: The core medieval realm of the Holy Roman Empire, formed from the eastern Frankish kingdom after the 843 Treaty of Verdun, whose kings claimed the imperial title from 962 onward.

east-francia.name: East Francia
east-francia.summary: A kingdom formed in 843 by dividing the Carolingian Empire, ruled by Carolingian kings until 911, that developed into the Kingdom of Germany.

otto-of-freising.name: Otto of Freising
otto-of-freising.summary: German churchman and bishop of Freising from 1138 (c. 1111–1158) who chronicled the political history of his time and took part in the Second Crusade.

charlemagne.name: Charlemagne
charlemagne.summary: King of the Franks from 768 and emperor of the Carolingian Empire from 800, who united most of Western and Central Europe and was the first recognised western emperor since Rome's fall.

frederick-barbarossa.name: Frederick Barbarossa
frederick-barbarossa.summary: Holy Roman Emperor from 1155 to 1190, also King of Germany, Italy and Burgundy; his Italian nickname "Barbarossa," meaning Red Beard, became one of history's most enduring monikers.
